title: How Prices Nudge You
objective: After this level you can spot common pricing tricks like prices ending in 99 and decoy options.
summary: Most shoppers don't know what a price should be, so cues steer them: a dress sold better at $39 than $34, and the word "sale" lifted demand. A decoy option can make its neighbor look like a bargain.

cards.headline: A dress sold better at $39 than at $34.
cards.body: In a catalog study by Eric Anderson and Duncan Simester, raising the price lifted demand by about a third. Higher price, more buyers. Something other than the number was doing the selling.

cards.headline: Why the 9 works
cards.body: For most things you buy, you don't really know what the price should be. Nobody carries the fair price of a dress around in their head. So shoppers lean on cues, signals that hint at a bargain, and a price ending in 9 is one of them. In the dress study, that little 9 did better than an actual $5 discount.

cards.headline: The word that sells
cards.body: Another cue is a single word. In catalog tests, putting "sale" beside a price increased demand by more than 50%. It works for the same reason as the 9: you can't easily check the price yourself, so the sign does the judging for you.

cards.headline: The option nobody buys
cards.body: Picture a coffee shop with a small for $3 and a large for $5. Now it adds a medium priced just under the large. Hardly anyone orders the medium, but suddenly the large looks like a steal. That's the decoy effect: adding a third, less attractive option changes how people choose between the original two. The decoy's job isn't to sell. It's to make its neighbor look brilliant.

mascot.line: The decoy is the friend who makes you look great in every photo.

cards.headline: Price tricks: spotted
learned: Shoppers rarely know what a price should be
Cues like 9-endings and "sale" signs steer them
A $39 dress outsold the same dress at $34
A decoy makes its neighbor look like a bargain

questions.prompt: In the catalog study, what happened when a dress's price rose from $34 to $39?

options.label: Demand fell by about a third
options.rationale: The surprise is that it went the other way.

options.label: Demand stayed the same
options.rationale: It changed, and in an unexpected direction.

options.label: Demand rose by about a third
The dress was withdrawn from sale
options.rationale: It stayed on sale and sold better.

questions.explanation: The higher price ending in 9 lifted demand by about a third.

questions.prompt: Hardly anyone orders the medium, priced just under the large. Why offer it?

options.label: It raises the price of the small
It makes the $5 large look like a bargain
It is meant to be the best seller
options.rationale: Hardly anyone orders it; that is the point.

options.label: It replaces the small
options.rationale: The small is still on the menu.

questions.explanation: A decoy is a less attractive option that changes how people choose between the other two.

questions.prompt: From Level 15: a 9-ending price nudges you to spend $39. What do economists call the next best thing that money could have bought?

options.label: A pricing cue
options.rationale: A cue is the nudge, not what you gave up.

options.label: A decoy
options.rationale: A decoy is an option meant to steer you.

questions.explanation: Whatever the $39 could otherwise have bought is the purchase's opportunity cost.
